items.question_text: A 46-year-old man attends a Darwin general practice for a repeat script. He mentions that his mother was Aboriginal. He has not had a health assessment. He is well, works, and has no chronic disease recorded. He identifies when asked. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Offer a 715 health assessment. Eligibility is by self-identification
Decline it. Urban residence removes eligibility
Require a certificate of Aboriginality before any discussion
Offer it only if she already has diabetes
Book it in 3 months because the interval is 6 months
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Offer a 715 health assessment. Eligibility is by self-identification

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A 46-year-old man attends a Darwin general practice for a repeat script. He mentions that his mother was Aboriginal. He has not had a health assessment.

2. THE RULE
The MBS 715 health assessment is offered on self-identification as Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander, no more than every 9 months, in the practice, not to an inpatient.

3. WHY A IS CORRECT
Item 715 is for a patient of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander descent, based on self-identification, at any age, in the community. Appearance, city residence, and the absence of a chronic disease do not decide it. It cannot be claimed if the same assessment was done in the preceding 9 months.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
B. Decline it. Urban residence removes eligibility: There is no urban exclusion.
C. Require a certificate of Aboriginality before any discussion: A certificate is not the Medicare test.
D. Offer it only if she already has diabetes: The assessment is preventive, not limited to known disease.
E. Book it in 3 months because the interval is 6 months: The claiming interval is 9 months, and she has never had one.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
The MBS 715 health assessment is offered on self-identification as Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander, no more than every 9 months, in the practice, not to an inpatient.

---

items.question_text: A 52-year-old Aboriginal woman asks for help with the cost of her PBS medicines. She has not been registered for Closing the Gap. She asks if she can register herself online. What is the most appropriate action?
options: He can self-register on the Services Australia app
A PBS prescriber or eligible Aboriginal Health Practitioner registers him once, after a clinical assessment
Registration is only available in remote clinics
He must already be on a concession card
Registration has to be repeated at every new pharmacy
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. A PBS prescriber or eligible Aboriginal Health Practitioner registers him once, after a clinical assessment

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
He needs a one-off clinical registration. He cannot sign himself up, and he does not need to live remotely.

2. THE RULE
Closing the Gap PBS co-payment eligibility requires a one-off registration by a PBS prescriber or eligible Aboriginal Health Practitioner before CTG scripts apply.

3. WHY B IS CORRECT
CTG PBS registration is done once, for life, by a PBS prescriber or an eligible Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Health Practitioner, through HPOS. The patient cannot self-register. It is not limited to remote areas or to concession-card holders, and it follows him across pharmacies.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. He can self-register on the Services Australia app: Patients cannot self-register.
C. Registration is only available in remote clinics: Location does not restrict it.
D. He must already be on a concession card: A concession card changes what he pays. It is not the entry rule.
E. Registration has to be repeated at every new pharmacy: One registration follows him.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
CTG PBS registration is one-off, by a prescriber or eligible health practitioner.

---

items.question_text: A 12-year-old boy in a remote clinic had acute rheumatic fever last year and is on secondary prophylaxis. His benzathine dose is due. A locum suggests oral penicillin for a week because the clinic is busy. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Oral amoxicillin for 5 days each month is first-line
Stop prophylaxis because the acute illness has settled
Give intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin, no later than 28 days after the last dose
Give daily erythromycin as the routine alternative
One benzathine dose now, then review in 12 months
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Give intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin, no later than 28 days after the last dose

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
She needs benzathine benzylpenicillin on a 28-day clock. Oral amoxicillin for 5 days a month is not secondary prophylaxis.

2. THE RULE
RHD secondary prophylaxis is IM benzathine benzylpenicillin every 28 days (weight-adjusted dose), with duration set by disease severity and overdue doses given promptly.

3. WHY C IS CORRECT
Intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin is first-line secondary prophylaxis, given no later than 28 days after the last dose. A 21-day interval is for breakthrough recurrence, not the routine start. Oral penicillin is less effective and is not the routine substitute. Erythromycin is for true penicillin hypersensitivity.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Oral amoxicillin for 5 days each month is first-line: Short oral courses are not secondary prophylaxis.
B. Stop prophylaxis because the acute illness has settled: The point of prophylaxis is to prevent the next episode.
D. Give daily erythromycin as the routine alternative: Macrolide is for hypersensitivity, which she does not have.
E. One benzathine dose now, then review in 12 months: The interval is 28 days, not a year.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
First-line secondary prophylaxis is intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin.

---

items.question_text: A 9-year-old in Townsville has fever, migratory arthritis, and a new murmur. You suspect acute rheumatic fever. A colleague says to wait for echocardiogram confirmation before notifying. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Notification is only required if he has severe carditis
Wait for the 6-week echocardiogram
Notification is the family's responsibility
Notify now and link him to the RHD control program
Notify only if a household contact develops a sore throat
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Notify now and link him to the RHD control program

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Definite acute rheumatic fever is notified now. The 6-week echocardiogram does not delay that.

2. THE RULE
Suspected acute rheumatic fever needs echocardiography, notification and register referral, and streptococcal infections in high-risk people are treated promptly.

3. WHY D IS CORRECT
Acute rheumatic fever is notifiable and the child should be registered with the jurisdictional RHD control program. The echocardiogram grades cardiac involvement. It does not gate the notification.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Notification is only required if he has severe carditis: Severity changes prophylaxis duration, not whether he is notified.
B. Wait for the 6-week echocardiogram: That loses the start of secondary prophylaxis and contact care.
C. Notification is the family's responsibility: It is a clinician and public-health duty.
E. Notify only if a household contact develops a sore throat: The case is notifiable regardless of contacts.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
ARF is notifiable on diagnosis.

---

items.question_text: A 15-year-old girl had acute rheumatic fever with moderate carditis three years ago. She has had no recurrence. Her mother asks if the benzathine can stop at five years for everyone. Moderate RHD means a longer course than a fixed five years. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Stop at 5 years because that is the universal rule
Stop now because adherence has been perfect
Switch to oral penicillin for the remaining years
Duration is decided by the family, not the echocardiogram
Continue according to the moderate-RHD duration, which is longer than the no-carditis rule
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Continue according to the moderate-RHD duration, which is longer than the no-carditis rule

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Moderate RHD does not stop at the no-carditis interval. His cousin's 5-year rule is the wrong line.

2. THE RULE
RHD secondary prophylaxis is IM benzathine benzylpenicillin every 28 days (weight-adjusted dose), with duration set by disease severity and overdue doses given promptly.

3. WHY E IS CORRECT
No-carditis disease is a minimum of 5 years or until 21, whichever is longer. Moderate RHD is a minimum of 10 years after the last ARF or until 35, whichever is longer. His cousin's rule does not apply to his valve.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Stop at 5 years because that is the universal rule: Five years is the no-carditis line.
B. Stop now because adherence has been perfect: Adherence is why it works. It is not a reason to stop early.
C. Switch to oral penicillin for the remaining years: Oral is not the routine remaining regimen.
D. Duration is decided by the family, not the echocardiogram: The family is part of the plan. The duration is clinical.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Prophylaxis duration follows cardiac severity.

---

items.question_text: An 8-year-old Aboriginal boy from a remote community has infected skin sores and tea-coloured urine. A colleague treats the sores and says no further action is needed. Skin sores in a high-risk child are treated, and acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is looked for and notified where required. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Assess and treat for acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis and notify
Reassure the family and review the sores in 2 weeks
Give topical mupirocin only
Start frusemide and send him home without bloods
APSGN does not follow skin infection, only pharyngitis
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Assess and treat for acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis and notify

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Puffy eyes, dark urine, and hypertension after skin sores is APSGN until proved otherwise. Do not wait 2 weeks.

2. THE RULE
Skin sores in a high-risk child are treated, APSGN is assessed and notified, and household contacts are examined for sores and scabies.

3. WHY A IS CORRECT
In northern and remote Australia, APSGN usually follows group A streptococcal skin infection. Oedema, dark urine, and hypertension in a child with sores is APSGN until assessed otherwise. It is notifiable in several jurisdictions and needs same-day clinical care, not a 2-week wait.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
B. Reassure the family and review the sores in 2 weeks: The renal signs are the emergency, not the crusts alone.
C. Give topical mupirocin only: Topical care does not treat APSGN.
D. Start frusemide and send him home without bloods: He needs assessment, not an unmonitored diuretic.
E. APSGN does not follow skin infection, only pharyngitis: In this setting skin is the usual source.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
APSGN in remote Australia usually follows skin infection.

---

items.question_text: A 55-year-old man from a Strongyloides-endemic northern community is about to start prednisolone for a flare of asthma. A colleague says to start the steroid and check serology later if he gets abdominal pain. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Start prednisolone. A normal eosinophil count excludes Strongyloides
Check Strongyloides serology or give pre-emptive ivermectin before immunosuppression
Stool microscopy alone is sensitive enough to clear him
Strongyloides is only a risk in returned travellers
Ivermectin is contraindicated if he has ever lived remotely
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Check Strongyloides serology or give pre-emptive ivermectin before immunosuppression

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A normal eosinophil count does not clear Strongyloides. Screen or give ivermectin before the steroids.

2. THE RULE
Before corticosteroids or immunosuppression in a person from a Strongyloides-endemic setting, check serology or give pre-emptive ivermectin.

3. WHY B IS CORRECT
Strongyloides is endemic in many remote northern communities. A normal eosinophil count does not exclude it, and stool microscopy is insensitive. Before immunosuppression he needs serology or pre-emptive ivermectin, because disseminated disease on steroids is dangerous.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Start prednisolone. A normal eosinophil count excludes Strongyloides: Eosinophilia is often absent.
C. Stool microscopy alone is sensitive enough to clear him: Stool microscopy misses most infections.
D. Strongyloides is only a risk in returned travellers: Northern Australian communities are endemic.
E. Ivermectin is contraindicated if he has ever lived remotely: Remote residence is the reason to consider it.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Strongyloides is endemic in remote northern Australia.

---

items.question_text: A 48-year-old man in Darwin presents in the wet season with severe pneumonia and sepsis. He works outdoors. He is deteriorating. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Ceftriaxone covers melioidosis, so continue it
Add gentamicin for northern Australian sepsis
Change to intravenous ceftazidime or meropenem and discuss melioidosis
Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate is sufficient intensive therapy
Wait for culture before changing antibiotics
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Change to intravenous ceftazidime or meropenem and discuss melioidosis

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Wet-season pneumonia and shock in a diabetic man in Darwin is melioidosis until proved otherwise. Use ceftazidime or meropenem.

2. THE RULE
Suspected melioidosis in tropical northern Australia is treated with IV ceftazidime or meropenem, not standard community pneumonia antibiotics.

3. WHY C IS CORRECT
Burkholderia pseudomallei is endemic in northern Australia, peaks in the wet season, and prefers people with diabetes. It is resistant to ceftriaxone and gentamicin. Intensive therapy is intravenous ceftazidime or meropenem. Waiting for culture in septic shock is the wrong delay.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Ceftriaxone covers melioidosis, so continue it: It does not.
B. Add gentamicin for northern Australian sepsis: The organism is intrinsically resistant to gentamicin.
D. Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate is sufficient intensive therapy: Oral therapy is the eradication phase, not the septic start.
E. Wait for culture before changing antibiotics: Septic shock in this setting is treated on suspicion.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Melioidosis peaks in the northern wet season and in people with diabetes.

---

items.question_text: A 34-year-old woman attends a city practice. The receptionist has marked her as non-Indigenous based on appearance. She has not been asked. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Leave it blank. Asking is offensive
Record Aboriginal because the clinic is near an Aboriginal service
Decide from skin colour
Ask the patient, in private, whether they identify as Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander
Only ask if the patient raises culture first
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Ask the patient, in private, whether they identify as Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Ask everyone, in private. Do not infer status from a surname, a suburb, or skin colour.

2. THE RULE
Indigenous status is asked of the patient, not assumed, and culturally safe care follows the patient's wishes without delaying urgent assessment.

3. WHY D IS CORRECT
Identification is by asking the person, not by appearance, surname, or suburb. The question is asked of everyone, privately, because it changes preventive care, Medicare items, and PBS access. Leaving it blank loses that care.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Leave it blank. Asking is offensive: Not asking is the error.
B. Record Aboriginal because the clinic is near an Aboriginal service: Proximity is not identity.
C. Decide from skin colour: Appearance is not the test.
E. Only ask if the patient raises culture first: The clinic asks. It does not wait.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Indigenous status is self-identified.

---

items.question_text: A 24-year-old pregnant woman with known rheumatic heart disease is booked for routine low-risk antenatal care at the local clinic. She has moderate mitral stenosis. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Routine shared care is enough because she feels well
Stop benzathine penicillin in pregnancy
Deliver at the local clinic because transfer is disruptive
RHD is not a pregnancy risk if the last echo was normal 3 years ago
Refer for specialist obstetric and cardiac care and restart secondary prophylaxis
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Refer for specialist obstetric and cardiac care and restart secondary prophylaxis

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Moderate RHD in pregnancy needs specialist care and continuous benzathine prophylaxis. Feeling well is not the clearance.

2. THE RULE
A pregnant woman with known RHD needs shared specialist obstetric and cardiac care and continued secondary prophylaxis, not routine low-risk care.

3. WHY E IS CORRECT
Pregnancy increases cardiac demand, and moderate RHD needs specialist planning, including place of birth. Missed benzathine doses should be restarted. Feeling well does not downgrade the risk, and a 3-year-old echo is not current.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Routine shared care is enough because she feels well: Symptoms lag behind risk.
B. Stop benzathine penicillin in pregnancy: Secondary prophylaxis continues in pregnancy.
C. Deliver at the local clinic because transfer is disruptive: Place of birth is a specialist decision.
D. RHD is not a pregnancy risk if the last echo was normal 3 years ago: Three years is not a current assessment.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Pregnancy is a high-risk setting for RHD.

---

items.question_text: A 6-year-old in a remote community has chronic discharge from one ear for months. A colleague says to watch it because it is common. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Treat the ear disease and arrange a hearing assessment
No action. Discharge is expected
Grommets tomorrow without treating the discharge
Tell the school the problem is behavioural
Oral amoxicillin for 3 days is a complete cure
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Treat the ear disease and arrange a hearing assessment

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Six weeks of ear discharge and a perforation needs treatment and a hearing check. It is not a normal finding to ignore.

2. THE RULE
Chronic suppurative otitis media in a remote child is actively treated with ear cleaning and topical antibiotics and the hearing is formally assessed.

3. WHY A IS CORRECT
Chronic suppurative otitis media is common and harmful. Six weeks of discharge with a perforation needs ear toilet, topical antibiotics, and a hearing assessment. It is not normal, and it is not a behaviour problem.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
B. No action. Discharge is expected: Expected does not mean acceptable.
C. Grommets tomorrow without treating the discharge: Operating on an untreated discharging ear is the wrong order.
D. Tell the school the problem is behavioural: The ear explains the classroom problem.
E. Oral amoxicillin for 3 days is a complete cure: CSOM needs topical therapy and ear care, not a short oral course.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Chronic suppurative otitis media is treated, not watched.

---

items.question_text: A child in a remote household has scabies and impetigo. The clinic has one tube of permethrin and the nurse plans to treat only the index child. What is the most appropriate action?

Treat the whole household for scabies and treat the impetigo
Oral ivermectin for the 4-year-old is always first-line
Antibiotics without scabies treatment will clear both
Scabies does not drive streptococcal skin infection
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Treat the whole household for scabies and treat the impetigo

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Treat the household for scabies and treat the sores. One tube for one child leaves the source in the house.

2. THE RULE
Scabies is treated in the whole household at the same time, with impetigo treated alongside, not just the index child.

3. WHY B IS CORRECT
Scabies is a household problem, and the breaks in the skin drive streptococcal impetigo, APSGN, and rheumatic fever. Contacts are treated at the same time. One index child is not the unit of treatment.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Treat only the index child: Untreated siblings reinfect her.
C. Oral ivermectin for the 4-year-old is always first-line: Weight, age, and pregnancy rules apply. It is not automatically first for every child.
D. Antibiotics without scabies treatment will clear both: The scabies remains.
E. Scabies does not drive streptococcal skin infection: It does, by breaking the skin.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Scabies is treated as a household.

Assess for serious infection, including meningitis, now
A fever in an Aboriginal man is always pneumonia
Confusion plus alcohol means no lumbar puncture is ever needed
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Assess for serious infection, including meningitis, now

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Fever, confusion, and neck stiffness are assessed now. The smell of alcohol is not the diagnosis.

2. THE RULE
Indigenous status is asked of the patient, not assumed, and culturally safe care follows the patient's wishes without delaying urgent assessment.

3. WHY C IS CORRECT
The smell of alcohol is a finding, not a diagnosis. Fever, confusion, and neck stiffness need immediate assessment for meningitis and other sepsis. Ethnicity does not choose the diagnosis.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Leave him in the corridor. The smell of alcohol is the diagnosis: This is the stereotype trap.
B. Discharge when he is sober: Sobriety does not treat meningitis.
D. A fever in an Aboriginal man is always pneumonia: That is another stereotype.
E. Confusion plus alcohol means no lumbar puncture is ever needed: Alcohol does not forbid the investigation he may need.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Do not let ethnicity or the smell of alcohol close the differential.

---

Do not wait until 45 and do not trust an unadjusted low-risk result. Assess and manage now.

2. THE RULE
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander adults have cardiovascular risk assessed from 30 years, and standard calculators may underestimate their risk.

3. WHY D IS CORRECT
Cardiovascular disease occurs earlier. Assessment and management start earlier than the general-population age, and an unadjusted calculator can underestimate risk. Waiting for chest pain is too late.

A. Wait until 45. The calculator is complete: The age and the unadjusted tool are both wrong here.
B. Risk assessment is not relevant before a myocardial infarct: The point is to act before the infarct.
C. Only check lipids if he develops chest pain: Symptoms are not the screening trigger.
E. Aboriginal status lowers cardiovascular risk: It raises it.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Cardiovascular risk is assessed earlier.

SAFE is surgery, antibiotics, facial cleanliness, environment.

items.question_text: A 14-year-old on benzathine secondary prophylaxis misses a dose by 10 days. A colleague restarts the whole course from zero and offers a short oral penicillin instead. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Stop prophylaxis. A missed dose ends the program
Give the overdue benzathine dose now and reset the 28-day clock
Replace the missed dose with 5 days of amoxicillin
He must restart a 10-year course from today
Ceremony is a contraindication to further injections
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Give the overdue benzathine dose now and reset the 28-day clock

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Give the late benzathine dose now and restart the 28-day interval. Do not abandon the program.

2. THE RULE
RHD secondary prophylaxis is IM benzathine benzylpenicillin every 28 days (weight-adjusted dose), with duration set by disease severity and overdue doses given promptly.

3. WHY B IS CORRECT
A late dose is given when he returns, and the next dose is 28 days from that injection. Ceremony is not a contraindication. A short oral course does not replace the injection, and one missed dose does not end the program.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Stop prophylaxis. A missed dose ends the program: Missed doses are recovered, not used to exit.
C. Replace the missed dose with 5 days of amoxicillin: Oral catch-up is not the regimen.
D. He must restart a 10-year course from today: The duration counts from the last ARF, not from one late dose.
E. Ceremony is a contraindication to further injections: Absence for ceremony is a reason to plan the next dose, not to stop.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
A late dose is given on return.

---

items.question_text: A child is diagnosed with acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. The family has several children at home. Treating only the index child is incomplete. What is the most appropriate action?
options: No contact action. APSGN is not transmissible
Exclude the whole community from school for a month
Ask the clinic to examine household children for sores, scabies, and signs of APSGN
Give the household a single dose of ceftriaxone
Only the mother needs a throat swab
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Ask the clinic to examine household children for sores, scabies, and signs of APSGN

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Tell the clinic to check the other children for sores, scabies, and APSGN. The streptococcus is the transmissible part.

2. THE RULE
Skin sores in a high-risk child are treated, APSGN is assessed and notified, and household contacts are examined for sores and scabies.

3. WHY C IS CORRECT
The streptococcus is transmissible. Household children need examination for sores, scabies, and early APSGN, and treatment of what is found. A month-long community exclusion and a household ceftriaxone dose are not the program.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. No contact action. APSGN is not transmissible: The immune disease is not caught. The streptococcus is.
B. Exclude the whole community from school for a month: Exclusion is for active sores until treated, not a community shutdown.
D. Give the household a single dose of ceftriaxone: That is not the contact regimen.
E. Only the mother needs a throat swab: Skin, not only the mother's throat, is the usual source.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
APSGN itself is immune-mediated. The streptococcus is what spreads.

---

Under 20 kg: 600,000 units. At or over 20 kg: 1,200,000 units.
